UPSTREAM: libpayload: Reset PS/2 keyboard Loading a libpayload based payload like coreinfo or FILO from SeaBIOS or GRUB pressing keys does not give the expected results. For example, pressing F1 gives the character 24 translated to scan code 6a. ESC for example 43 (111) in coreinfo loaded from SeaBIOS on QEMU Q35. The problem is not reproducible using the payload directly, that means without SeaBIOS or GRUB. The problem seems to be, that those have already initialized the PS/2 controller and AT keyboard. Comparing it with coreboots PS/2 keyboard code, the keyboard needs to be reset. That seems to fix the issue, when the keyboard was initialized before. TEST=Build coreboot for QEMU Q35 with SeaBIOS, and coreinfo as secondary payload. Run qemu-system-i386 -M q35 -L /dev/shm -bios build/coreboot.rom -serial stdio press 3 to select the coreinfo payload, and verify that the keys F1 and F2 are working. Same with coreinfo loaded from GRUB on the ASRock E350M1. UPSTREAM: intel/sandybridge: Make timC training more robust. When using native raminit with https://review.coreboot.org/#/c/22683/ I've found that timC training usually fails unless the ram is overspecced (i.e. DDR3L-1600 rated for 1.35V works most of the time with native raminit as DDR3-1333 @1.5V). Looking at the training data I've found that during timC training it is reading register values in the 0-4000 range and checking for runs of 0, but with the failing training the values don't go all the way down to 0. The solution for me has been to do a thresholing pre-pass, after which both the DDR3-1333 @1.5V and the DDR3L-1600 @1.35V work fine for me. Tested: - Intel NUC DCP847SKE - RAM slots with 2x4GB Kingston KVR1333D3S9/4G (DDR3-1333 1.5V), boots fine with native raminit @1.5V - RAM slots with 2x4GB Kingston KVR16LS11/4G (DDR3L-1600 1.35V), boots fine with native raminit @1.35V - Casual use with these settings - Tested on Lenovo T520 with Crucial HyperX DDR3-1833. - Memtest86+ stable. FROMLIST: PM / OPP: Support adjusting OPP voltages at runtime On some SoCs the Adaptive Voltage Scaling (AVS) technique is employed to optimize the operating voltage of a device. At a given frequency, the hardware monitors dynamic factors and either makes a suggestion for how much to adjust a voltage for the current frequency, or it automatically adjusts the voltage without software intervention. Add an API to the OPP library for the former case, so that AVS type devices can update the voltages for an OPP when the hardware determines the voltage should change. The assumption is that drivers like CPUfreq or devfreq will register for the OPP notifiers and adjust the voltage according to suggestions that AVS makes. This patch is devired from [1] submitted by Stephen. Revert "CHROMIUM: scripts: Use savedefconfig to minimize kernel config" This reverts commit 488fac42d2fe78393599da77e5e25828c15e3deb. The 3.x kernels have an environment variable, WIFIVERSION, that affects which subtree is used during kconfig and build. This is a per-board setting configured by a USE flag (eg USE=wireless34). What this means is our kernel configs are generated and normalized based on the base wireless/ tree, but then different boards are built against wireless trees with a different Kconfig structure. This sort of works today by luck if most of the Kconfigs have the same names, and we're fine with the silent defaulted values for any of the ones that are unique. My minimization change perturbs the system more by not listing kconfigs that come by default or via select. This allows more things to change when we swap out a completely different tree at build time than we configured for. For instance, the minimized version is now sensitive to changes in depends and select between the trees, where the haystack version had a better chance to work out since it listed everything. Back out the splitconfig minimization for 3.x kernels, as those seem to be held together in a very fragile way, and the benefit of consistency doesn't outweigh the risk of destabilization. Revert "CHROMIUM: scripts: Use savedefconfig to minimize kernel config" This reverts commit eb4733ee24c6f6107ca7f4795018b035f9f86809. The 3.x kernels have an environment variable, WIFIVERSION, that affects which subtree is used during kconfig and build. This is a per-board setting configured by a USE flag (eg USE=wireless34). What this means is our kernel configs are generated and normalized based on the base wireless/ tree, but then different boards are built against wireless trees with a different Kconfig structure. This sort of works today by luck if most of the Kconfigs have the same names, and we're fine with the silent defaulted values for any of the ones that are unique. My minimization change perterbs the system more by not listing kconfigs that come by default or via select. This allows more things to change when we swap out a completely different tree at build time than we configured for. For instance, the minimized version is now sensitive to changes in depends and select between the trees, where the haystack version had a better chance to work out since it listed everything. Back out the splitconfig minimization for 3.x kernels, as those seem to be held together in a very fragile way, and the benefit of consistency doesn't outweigh the risk of destabilization. shill: routing: Allow specifying an allocated table as per-device Per-device routing tables let us employ the power of policy-based routing in choosing which device to use for outgoing network traffic of particular characteristics. Scenarios like "only send traffic out of interface N if the packets have source address X" or "prefer to send traffic with fwmark Y out of interface M" cannot be achieved using only routes in the main routing table. The RoutingTable code prior to this change allows for the creation of new kernel routing tables for use in policy based routing (at least from the perspective of the user). However, these plainly-allocated routing tables are not suitable for use as per-device routing tables. In particular, routing table entries that come from outside of shill (e.g. entries added by the kernel on receipt of IPv6 router advertisements, or for setting up default routes to a specific gateway) still go to the main routing table. This change allows for a table to be specified as the per-device table for a particular interface. When this is performed, routing table entries for that interface will be placed into the per-device table rather than in a different table.
